key_terms.meaning: The software layer (also called virtual machine monitor) that creates, runs and schedules virtual machines on one physical host.
The real physical machine — its CPU, RAM, disks and NICs — on which the hypervisor and its guests run.
The OS installed inside a virtual machine; it believes it owns real hardware.
A schedulable software copy of a physical core that the hypervisor gives to a guest.
Assigning guests more vCPU or memory than the host physically has, relying on the fact that not all guests use it at once.
Splitting one physical machine into several isolated execution environments so workloads cannot interfere.
A fault or attack inside one VM stays inside it and cannot read or corrupt another VM's memory or disk.
A whole VM state lives in ordinary files, so it can be copied, backed up or moved like any file.
A VM image runs on any host with a compatible hypervisor, whatever the underlying brand of server.
A privileged instruction from a guest traps into the hypervisor, which emulates the effect and returns to the guest.
The hypervisor rewrites guest kernel instruction blocks at run time, replacing sensitive instructions with safe calls, so the guest need not be modified.
A deliberate call from a modified guest kernel to the hypervisor, like a system call but aimed at the VMM.
Instructions that read or change privileged machine state; a guest must not execute them directly on the host CPU.
Hardware transitions: VM exit leaves the guest for the hypervisor, VM entry returns control to the guest.
Hypervisor-maintained guest-to-machine page tables that keep a guest's idea of physical addresses honest.
Intel Extended Page Tables and AMD Nested Page Tables: hardware that translates guest-physical to host-physical addresses in a second level.
A cooperative guest driver that hands memory pages back to the hypervisor when the host is short of RAM.
A standard para-virtual I/O interface in which the guest and hypervisor share ring buffers instead of emulating a real device.
A Linux kernel feature that gives a process group its own private view of PIDs, network, mounts or hostname.
A Linux control group that caps and accounts the CPU, memory and I/O a set of processes may use.

takeaways: Virtualization puts a software layer between hardware and operating systems so one machine behaves as many isolated machines.
The hypervisor is the piece that partitions, schedules and isolates, and it can sit at hardware, OS, library or application level.
Full virtualization runs an unmodified guest using trap-and-emulate or binary translation; para-virtualization runs a modified guest that makes hypercalls.
CPU, memory and I/O each need their own virtualization trick: vCPU scheduling, two-level address translation, and shared or assigned devices.
Hardware assists such as EPT, NPT and IOMMU remove most of the cost of trapping, which is why virtualization became cheap and common.
Storage virtualization hides many disks behind one logical pool; network virtualization hides physical links behind logical ones.
A VM carries a full guest OS and boots in minutes; a container shares the host kernel and starts in under a second.
Containers are just processes held apart by namespaces and held in check by cgroups, which is why they are lighter but less isolated than VMs.
A virtual cluster or virtual data centre is a tenant's logical view built out of VMs, virtual disks and virtual networks on shared hardware.
Xen, VMware ESXi and Hyper-V all differ in where the control logic lives, but all three are Type 1 hypervisors running guests directly on the metal.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to define virtualization, classify it by level, compare full and para-virtualization, trace CPU-memory-I/O mechanisms, and finish with a VM-versus-container comparison plus one named hypervisor case study.

bank.q: Define virtualization and explain partitioning, isolation, encapsulation and hardware independence with one example each.
outline: Definition of a software layer between hardware and OS
Partitioning: many VMs on one host
Isolation: faults and data stay inside a VM
Encapsulation: VM saved as files, so copy and migrate
Hardware independence: same image on any compatible host
One concrete example per property

bank.q: List the pros and cons of virtualization in a data centre.
outline: Pros: server consolidation, lower power and space cost, fast provisioning, snapshots and live migration, legacy OS support
Cons: hypervisor overhead, single point of failure, VM sprawl, licensing cost, complexity of management, security of the hypervisor itself

bank.q: Explain the taxonomy of virtualization techniques by implementation level.
outline: Hardware level: hypervisor directly on the metal or on a host OS
Operating-system level: one kernel, many isolated containers
Library level: a library intercepts API calls, e.g. WINE
Application level: a process-level runtime such as the JVM
Compare overhead and isolation strength across the four levels

bank.q: What is a hypervisor? Distinguish Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors and give one example of each.
outline: Definition and role: create, schedule, isolate VMs
Type 1 bare-metal: runs on hardware, guest sits above it
Type 2 hosted: runs as an application on a host OS
Examples: Xen, ESXi, Hyper-V for Type 1; VirtualBox, VMware Workstation for Type 2
Effect on performance and use case

bank.q: Compare full virtualization with para-virtualization in terms of guest modification, mechanism and performance.
outline: Full: unmodified guest, hypervisor hidden
Mechanism: trap and emulate, or binary translation when traps are hard
Para: guest kernel modified to issue hypercalls
Para avoids most traps, so lower overhead on I/O
Full works with any OS, para needs a ported OS
Mention sensitive instructions and why they must be controlled

bank.q: Describe how the hypervisor virtualizes the CPU.
outline: vCPU as a schedulable entity
Guest instructions run natively on the host core most of the time
Privileged and sensitive instructions cause a VM exit
Hypervisor emulates, then VM entry resumes the guest
vCPU scheduling and overcommit
Hardware virtualization extensions reduce exit cost

bank.q: Explain memory virtualization using shadow page tables and hardware second-level translation.
outline: Guest virtual to guest physical to host physical mapping
Shadow page tables maintained by hypervisor, cost of keeping them in sync
EPT and NPT add a second translation level in hardware
Fewer VM exits, so lower overhead
Page sharing to deduplicate identical pages
Balloon driver for reclaiming memory under pressure

bank.q: Explain I/O virtualization, including direct assignment, IOMMU, SR-IOV and Virtio.
outline: Emulated device: simple but slow, every access traps
Para-virtual device such as Virtio: shared ring buffers, batched access
Direct assignment gives a VM the real device
IOMMU gives DMA isolation and safe interrupts
SR-IOV gives many virtual functions from one physical device
Trade-off between throughput, sharing and isolation

bank.q: Compare a virtual machine with a Docker container.
outline: VM: hypervisor plus full guest OS, strong isolation, GB image, boot in minutes
Container: shares host kernel, uses namespaces for isolation and cgroups for limits
Container image layered and small, starts in under a second
Density and overhead comparison
Weaker isolation boundary for containers
Typical use: containers for microservices, VMs for heterogeneous OS and hard isolation

bank.q: Explain namespaces and cgroups and how Docker uses them.
outline: Namespace = private view of a global resource; PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user
cgroup = accounting and limit on CPU, memory, block I/O
Docker creates namespaces and a cgroup per container
Layered image built from a Dockerfile and shared between containers
Result: a process that looks like its own small machine

bank.q: A server with 16 cores and 64 GB RAM must host 20 small web application VMs. Show how overcommit and vCPU scheduling let you plan the placement, and state the risk.
outline: Work out per-VM vCPU and memory share under overcommit
Explain that vCPUs are time-sliced, not dedicated
Explain memory ballooning and page sharing to relieve pressure
Risk: contention, noisy neighbour, swap inside guest, latency spikes
Recommend reserving resources for the busiest VMs

bank.q: Design storage and network virtualization for a private cloud serving three departments, naming the components and the isolation you would use.
outline: Pool physical disks into logical volumes presented to VMs
Thin provisioning, snapshots and clones for fast copies
Virtual switches and VLAN or overlay segments per department
Tenant-level separation of traffic and of volumes
Software-defined control plane to configure both from one place
Measure isolation and failure containment

bank.q: Analyse why trap-and-emulate fails for some instructions and how binary translation and hardware assists fix it.
outline: Classify instructions as privileged, sensitive or innocuous
Some sensitive instructions do not trap, so emulation is not triggered
Binary translation rewrites those blocks before execution
Hardware virtualization adds a guest mode and exit reasons
Cost model: number of exits per unit of work
Conclusion: choose the mechanism by workload type

bank.q: A team must deploy fifty microservices. Evaluate VMs against containers on isolation, density, startup time and operational effort, and recommend a design.
outline: Isolation: VM boundary stronger, container shares kernel
Density: containers pack far more per host
Startup: seconds versus minutes, so scaling differs
Operational effort: image build, registry, orchestration
Security: kernel bug reaches all containers on the host
Recommendation: containers for the services, VMs as the tenant boundary

glossary.def: Presenting one physical resource as several isolated logical resources through a software layer.
A software-defined computer with its own virtual CPU, memory, disks and NICs, running a full guest OS.
Another name for the hypervisor: the layer that creates and supervises VMs.
A hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware with no host OS beneath it.
A hypervisor that runs as an application on top of a conventional host OS.
Running an unmodified guest OS while hiding the hypervisor's existence from it.
Running a modified guest OS that cooperates with the hypervisor through hypercalls.
A controlled call made by a para-virtual guest kernel into the hypervisor.
In Xen, the privileged first VM that holds the drivers and management tools.
Moving a running VM to another host with only a brief pause, using its encapsulated memory image.
A point-in-time saved state of a VM's disk and memory that can be restored or cloned.
Allocating more virtual resources than the host physically owns.
Storing one physical copy of identical memory pages used by several VMs.
An input-output memory management unit that translates and isolates device DMA addresses.
Single Root I/O Virtualization: one physical device exposes several virtual functions, each assignable to a VM.
Pooling physical disks into logical volumes that are presented to VMs independently of the hardware.
A network whose forwarding rules are set by software control planes rather than by fixed device configuration.
A virtual network built as tunnels over an existing physical network.
An isolated group of processes sharing the host kernel, packaged with its own filesystem view.
A read-only layered filesystem template from which containers are started.
A kernel feature giving a process group a private view of a global resource such as PIDs or the network stack.
A kernel control group that limits and accounts the resources a process set may consume.
A logical cluster of VMs on shared hosts that behaves like a dedicated cluster to its users.
A tenant's logical view of compute, storage and network resources drawn from shared physical infrastructure.
